title_en: On Himself and the See of Constantinople
author: Gregory of Nazianzus
addressee: The congregation and people of Constantinople
occasion: Gregory responds to those who say he desired the episcopal throne of Constantinople, and addresses the people's passionate attachment to him after they forcibly installed him on the throne, an act he describes as lawbreaking done in zeal and anger.
argument: Gregory marvels at the people's love for him and his preaching, attributing it not to his own wisdom but to their prior faith and to God. He explains their affection as a response to his moderation, his suffering, and his defense of orthodox teaching. He denies desiring the see, presenting himself as a guardian and steward who will give the church away in marriage to another if he proves worthy of her beauty. He then exhorts the people to hold fast to the orthodox confession of the Trinity and to live virtuously, addressing various groups in the city.

outline.move: Gregory wonders at the people's attachment to him and his preaching, disclaiming any special wisdom and tracing their faith to the teaching of Alexander.
He denies using flattery or theatrical methods, and recalls how the people in zeal and anger forcibly placed him on the throne, an act he calls a novelty and the throne itself tyrannical.

He offers three reasons for the people's love: their own choice of him, his quiet and philosophical manner, and their pity mixed with respect for his sufferings; he then reflects on envy as the source of his troubles.

He argues by analogy that if he were helping a storm-tossed ship, besieged city, or burning house, he would be called a protector and guardian, not a wrecker or lover of the thing itself, and that he cares more for God's judgment than for human opinion.
He urges the people to be his defense by keeping the orthodox confession of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit and by living virtuously.
He addresses emperors, courtiers, the well-born, the learned, the rich, the self-indulgent, and the city of Constantinople, exhorting each to virtue and closing with a doxology.

cast.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
cast.who: The speaker, bishop recently installed in Constantinople, defending himself against those who say he desired the see.

cast.name: Alexander of Alexandria
cast.who: The great champion and herald of the Trinity, whose teaching the people of Constantinople followed.

cast.name: Paul the Apostle
cast.who: Quoted as an apostolic authority for the speaker's conduct and hopes.

cast.name: Moses
cast.who: Old Testament figure cited for bringing forth water in the desert.

cast.name: Isaac
cast.who: Patriarch whose servants not only dug wells of living water but also cleared those stopped up by the Philistines.

cast.name: Daniel
cast.who: Prophet cited for the lawlessness that came from elders in Babylon.

cast.name: Jeroboam
cast.who: Old Testament rebel figure, here applied to Gregory's opponent, called the slave of sin, who puts a bond on Gregory's tongue.

cast.name: Rehoboam
cast.who: King criticized for following the counsel of the young rather than the elders.

cast.name: Lazarus
cast.who: The poor man of the Gospel parable, held up as a model for care of the poor.

voices.speaker: Gregory's opponents
voices.how_marked: Introduced by φησί or φησὶ with their objection; appears three times in section 4, with objections about popular opinion (twice) and about shame at Gregory's humiliations (once).

voices.speaker: Paul the Apostle
voices.how_marked: Introduced by φησὶν ὁ Παῦλος or φησὶν ὁ θεῖος Ἀπόστολος. Note: In section 1, the quotation 'You are witnesses, and God' does not match any known Pauline text exactly; it may be a paraphrase or conflation.

voices.speaker: Scripture
voices.how_marked: Introduced by ἀκούσατε τοῦ λέγοντος or ἤκουσας τῆς Γραφῆς λεγούσης

key_terms.sense: The episcopal throne or see of Constantinople, the object of the disputed desire.
Right doctrine, specifically the confession of the Trinity.
The Trinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the central confession Gregory defends.
The single divine nature shared by Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
Envy, the destructive passion Gregory identifies as the source of his troubles and of many biblical disasters.
The quiet, moderate, contemplative way of life Gregory claims for himself.
The church, here personified as a widow in need of a guardian until a worthy bridegroom appears.
The confession of faith in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit that the people must keep unshaken.
The way of life or conduct that must match right doctrine.
Virtue, the excellence Gregory urges on all groups in the city.
The sacred ministry or worship, contrasted with the theater.
The purple robe, symbol of imperial authority.

scripture: Gregory uses the Septuagint (LXX) text and its book names and Psalm numbering. Citations should be given in modern English form, using standard Protestant book names and Psalm numbering where they differ from the LXX.
uncertain: The precise date of delivery within Gregory's time in Constantinople.
The exact identity of the 'apostate tyrant' mentioned in section 3.
Whether the 'Jeroboam' opponent in section 3 refers to a specific contemporary figure or is a general type.
Whether the Pauline quotation in section 1 is a paraphrase or conflation rather than a direct quotation.

_unresolved_facts.claim: an act he describes as lawbreaking done in zeal and anger
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐθήκατε δ' οὖν, διὰ τὸν πόθον παρανομήσαντες
_unresolved_facts.fix: the people forcibly installed him on the throne, breaking the law out of desire/love (πόθος), not anger; the anger belongs to the people earlier in the context (ζήλῳ καὶ θυμῷ ζέσαντες) but the lawbreaking is attributed to πόθος

_unresolved_facts.claim: He denies desiring the see, presenting himself as a guardian and steward who will give the church away in marriage to another if he proves worthy of her beauty
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἄλλῳ νυμφαγω γήσοντες, ὃς ἐὰν ἄξιος τοῦ κάλλους φανῇ, καὶ πλείο να τὰ ἐξ ἀρετῆς ἔδνα προσενέγκῃ τῇ βασιλίδι
_unresolved_facts.fix: he presents himself as a guardian and steward who will give the church away in marriage to another if that other proves worthy of her beauty and brings more dowry of virtue

_unresolved_facts.claim: He denies using flattery or theatrical methods, and recalls how the people in zeal and anger forcibly placed him on the throne, an act he calls a novelty and the throne itself tyrannical
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: τὸν οὐκ οἶδ' εἴτε τυραννικὸν χρὴ λέγειν, εἴτε ἀρχιερατικόν
_unresolved_facts.fix: he calls the throne itself 'I don't know whether to call it tyrannical or archiepiscopal,' not definitively 'tyrannical'; the uncertainty is important

_unresolved_facts.claim: He argues by analogy that if he were helping a storm-tossed ship, besieged city, or burning house, he would be called a protector and guardian, not a wrecker or lover of the thing itself
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὡς δὴ σύ γε, ὦ βέλτιστε, καὶ εἰ νηῒ χειμαζομένῃ χεῖρα ὀρέγομεν
_unresolved_facts.fix: the analogy is introduced with ὡς δὴ σύ γε ('as you, best one, [would say] even if...'), suggesting this is his response to an interlocutor's objection, not simply his own argument; the 'you' is his opponent

_unresolved_facts.claim: Isaac ... whose servants not only dug wells of living water but also cleared those stopped up by the Philistines
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: κατὰ τοὺς παῖδας Ἰσαὰκ τοῦ μεγά λου, μὴ ὀρύσσοντας μόνον φρέατα ζῶντος ὕδα τος, ἀλλὰ καὶ φρασσόμενα ὑπὸ τῶν Φυλιστιαίων ἀνα καθαίροντας
_unresolved_facts.fix: the text says 'according to the children/servants of Isaac the great, not only digging wells of living water but also clearing those stopped up by the Philistines' — but these are Isaac's servants/children, not Isaac himself; the brief is correct about the servants but should note Gregory presents himself as doing what Isaac's servants did

_unresolved_facts.claim: Paul the Apostle ... In section 1, the quotation 'You are witnesses, and God' does not match any known Pauline text exactly; it may be a paraphrase or conflation
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ὑμεῖς μάρτυρες, καὶ ὁ Θεός, φησὶν ὁ θεῖος Ἀπόστολος
_unresolved_facts.fix: the quotation 'You are witnesses, and God' is introduced as spoken by 'the divine Apostle' but this is not a Pauline quotation; it appears to be Gregory's own words or a free formulation, not a scriptural citation. The note about it being a 'paraphrase or conflation' is speculative; better to say it is not identifiable as a Pauline text and may be Gregory's own formulation attributed to the Apostle's spirit

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ὑμεῖς μάρτυρες, καὶ ὁ Θεός, φησὶν ὁ θεῖος Ἀπόστολος
_unresolved_facts.fix: the 'divine Apostle' in section 1 is not clearly Paul; the quotation does not match Paul. In section 5, φησὶν ὁ Παῦλος introduces a clear Pauline allusion (1 Thess 2:19-20). Section 1 should be marked as uncertain or not Pauline

_unresolved_facts.claim: Gregory's opponents ... appears three times in section 4, with objections about popular opinion (twice) and about shame at Gregory's humiliations (once)
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἀλλ' αἰσχυνόμεθά σου, φησὶ, ταῖς ὕβρεσιν
_unresolved_facts.fix: the third objection about shame at humiliations is in section 4, but the opponents say 'we are ashamed at your insults/humiliations' (ὕβρεσιν), not 'shame at Gregory's humiliations' — this is ambiguous; it could mean they are ashamed BY the insults he suffers, or ashamed OF his (alleged) insulting behavior. The context suggests the former (pity for his humiliation), but the Greek is 'your insults' not 'your humiliations'
